articles.title: A cattle rancher voted for Trump. But now he's 'had enough of this crap'
articles.summary: The president’s policies have given whiplash to farmers and ranchers in red states — including in swing districts. Will it matter in the midterms?
articles.body:
MISSOULA, MT – Wally Congdon is done with Donald Trump .

The 69-year-old cattle rancher, a member of the Montana Cowboy Hall of Fame, voted for him in 2024 amid frustrations with the Biden administration's immigration agenda. He also supported Rep. Ryan Zinke, a Republican retiring from Congress this year.

Two years later, turmoil in the Middle East has sent diesel prices soaring to record highs. Fertilizer costs have skyrocketed, too. The president's trade wars, including with neighboring Canada, are raging. And Trump has repeatedly moved against the wishes of many of his GOP allies to import more foreign beef , undercutting domestic producers like Congdon, who raises highland cows about 30 miles east of his home in Missoula.

"We've had enough of this crap," Congdon said. This fall, he wants to send a Democrat to represent him in Washington instead.

Independent-minded voters like Congdon are part of what has made the race for Montana's western congressional district unexpectedly competitive – and it's not alone. Similar dynamics are playing out in other contests across the country, putting into play red-state seats that Republicans earlier this year considered for months to be comparatively safe bets.

While farmers and ranchers have for decades been a relatively reliably conservative voting bloc in many cases – and there's no indication that's fundamentally changing – there has been wide acknowledgment among the agricultural community that the Trump administration's mercurial policies are taking a toll. Even if the whiplash has just a marginal impact in swing districts, it could make a difference in the midterms.

In Montana, Democrat Sam Forstag, a union leader and former smokejumper who has notched Congdon's vote, is in a neck-and-neck race against Aaron Flint, a Trump-endorsed veteran and conservative radio host. Montana hasn't elected a Democrat to the House of Representatives since 1994, but in September the nonpartisan elections handicapper the Cook Political Report moved the district from "likely Republican" to "lean Republican." This month, the race became even closer when Cook shifted it to a "toss-up."

"I'm very depressed to tell you Montana 1 is listed as a toss-up," Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson told a group of Republicans at a Flint campaign event in the city of Bozeman last week.

In an interview with USA TODAY, Flint agreed that farmers and ranchers are hurting. He even broke with Trump recently, opposing the president's foreign beef import efforts .

Still, Flint argued, livestock producers were much worse off during the Biden years. He touted his own endorsement from the Montana Stockgrowers Association, the state's most powerful ag lobby, and he promised to loosen regulations on his farm-owning constituents.

"They know that I'm going to be somebody who's going to have their back," Flint said.

A convergence of issues is uniquely testing the loyalty of farmers and ranchers to Republicans this election cycle.

For one thing, Trump's penchant for tariffs has hiked supply costs while threatening the export markets that producers rely on to make a living.

Steve Sheffels, a wheat farmer and the president of the Montana Grain Growers Association, said he hasn't bought a new combine since 2013. Trump's steel tariffs have made replacing many pieces of equipment that people like him need more expensive.

"The price of parts at the store is ridiculous," he said.

Conflicts overseas have made life even harder lately in cattle country. The war in Iran has disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for global oil markets. The regional tumult has dramatically raised the price of both fertilizer, which often requires natural gas to make, and diesel, the fuel on which America's farms largely run.

Sheffels said a friend of his was paying about $3,500 a week just for fuel during the winter wheat harvest this year.

It's all happening as ranchers are already trying to recover from a yearslong period of shifting weather patterns, including severe drought, that have worsened pasture conditions and left lingering impacts.

As the overall U.S. beef and dairy cattle herd hit a 75-year low, prices went up, making groceries more broadly expensive for Americans. In hopes of making staples like steak and hamburger more affordable, Trump signed a decree in September to ease tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef imports to be sold below market value. It followed a similar move in February, when he lifted tariffs on beef from Argentina .

Both decisions angered livestock producers and congressional Republicans alike.

Ben Peterson, a rancher in the roughly 100-person town of Judith Gap, Montana, said he likely lost about $5,000 due to the pricing pressure Trump's latest import announcement put on the cattle market. Other ranchers told USA TODAY in August they, too, were missing out on hundreds of dollars per cow at the auction barn.

Peterson, a Democrat, lives in the eastern part of the state, where Montana's other Republican congressman, Troy Downing, is cruising to reelection. He was skeptical that the recent instability would push many ranchers to vote for Democrats.

Disillusionment with Trump, though, has clearly grown among livestock producers, he said.

"They're more likely to just sit out," he said.

With the midterms in sight, Trump and Vice President JD Vance have been barnstorming the campaign trail in red states, including with trips to Montana.

During an Oct. 14 rally in the mountain town of Kalispell, Trump stressed that he and GOP lawmakers passed legislation last year to eliminate estate taxes for family farms. He also suggested that Chinese President Xi Jinping promised he'd be "doubling up on his purchases from the farmers."

"We're never going to let our farmers get hurt," Trump said.

In recent weeks, the White House announced a flurry of new agricultural policies. Among them was an $8 billion Department of Agriculture program offering one-time payments to offset high diesel costs from this fall's harvest. The president also penned an order to loosen rules on off-road, cheaper diesel. And top federal officials are reportedly working toward a detente in the trade war with Canada.

Walter Schweitzer, president of the Montana Farmers Union, likened some of those measures, however, to "pissing on a forest fire."

Zachary Schermele is the congressional correspondent for USA TODAY. Reach him by email at zschermele@usatoday.com and on Signal @zachschermele.02. Follow him on X at @ZachSchermele.

articles.title: Poll: Crowley favored over Tiffany in Wisconsin governor's race
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – Democrat David Crowley leads Republican Tom Tiffany with 51% of the vote compared to 44% for Tiffany, according to a new Marquette Law...
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – Democrat David Crowley leads Republican Tom Tiffany with 51% of the vote compared to 44% for Tiffany, according to a new Marquette Law School Poll.

The poll showed that 47% of all registered voters preferred Crowley with 44% for Tiffany, falling within the polls margin of error.

The survey was conducted Oct. 14-22, interviewing 818 Wisconsin registered voters, with a margin of error of +/-4.3 percentage points. For likely voters, the sample size is 668 with a margin of error of +/-4.7 percentage points.

"We've seen a pretty close race over the fall," Marquette Law School Poll Director Charles Franklin said.

The poll is the final for Marquette before Tuesday's election.

None of Marquette's polling showed Crowley as the favorite over Francesca Hong in the tumultuous Democratic primary where Crowley dropped out and later re-entered the race when Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez dropped out.

The poll showed that Democrats are more likely to vote than Republicans with 84% of Democrats being likely to vote and 77% of Republicans.

The poll showed that Tiffany's plan to have a 10% cut in income tax for families that make $150,000 or less, ending taxes on tips and overtime was very popular with 83% of voters approving the plan and 49% saying that they strongly favor it.

Polling was closer on Tiffany's plan to return the state's more than $3 billion surplus to voters with 76% of Republicans preferring to return the surplus with 77% of Democrats favoring using it for services along with 58% of independent voters.

Tiffany was seen as the candidate who would do more to reduce taxes while voters believed Crowley would do more to make healthcare more affordable, improve education and improve data center policy.

articles.title: Lula cresce em regiões metropolitanas; Flávio perde votos em sete | G1
articles.standfirst: Dados do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral mostram como a votação dos candidatos variou do 1º para o 2º turno da disputa presidencial nas grandes cidades e no entorno. Veja também comparação entre desempenho de Flávio em 2026 e de Jair Bolsonaro em 2022.
articles.summary: No segundo turno das eleições 2026, Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro tiveram desempenhos opostos nas regiões metropolitanas, com o petista crescendo em 77 das 78 áreas.
articles.body:
Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro — Foto: REUTERS/Adriano Machado

Reeleito presidente no 2º turno das eleições de 2026, Lula (PT) reverteu o placar em três das 78 regiões metropolitanas brasileiras e ampliou sua votação em mais de 30% em outras seis, na comparação com o 1º turno. Derrotado na disputa, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) viu sua votação recuar em sete regiões metropolitanas, que incluem grandes cidades e municípios de seu entorno, segundo dados do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE).

Veja os números por região e sua variação do 1º para o 2º turno abaixo na reportagem.

Já Flávio teve crescimento de dois dígitos em apenas três regiões metropolitanas:

Na região metropolitana de São Paulo, o crescimento de 11% na votação de Flávio Bolsonaro não foi suficiente para superar Lula, que ampliou seu número de votos em 26,89% do primeiro para o segundo turno. Os dois candidatos tiveram votações próximas na capital paulista e nos municípios do entorno.

O presidente eleito conquistou 1,4 milhão de votos adicionais na Grande São Paulo, passando de 5,3 milhões para 6,7 milhões. Já o senador ganhou 585 mil votos, passando de 5,1 milhões para 5,7 milhões.

Entre as regiões metropolitanas das capitais, os maiores crescimentos proporcionais na votação de Lula foram registrados em Goiânia (36,42%), Curitiba (27,73%), São Paulo (26,89%), Belo Horizonte (25,57%) e Porto Alegre (23,84%).

Já Flávio Bolsonaro registrou seus maiores crescimentos de votação nas regiões metropolitanas de Goiânia (17,38%), São Paulo (11,35%), Curitiba (10,78%), Belo Horizonte (9,74%) e Porto Alegre (9,33%).

Lula perdeu votos entre o primeiro e o segundo turno em apenas uma das 78 regiões metropolitanas brasileiras, a Central de Roraima, enquanto Flávio Bolsonaro registrou queda na votação em sete delas:

Central (RR): -14,67% (Lula recuou -2,45%);

Sul do Estado (RR): -10,86% (Lula cresceu 3,69%)

Zona Leste do Estado do Maranhão (MA): -0,23%

Resultados de 1º e 2º turno nas regiões metropolitanas em 2026 — Foto: Arte/g1

Os dados mostram que o vencedor foi o mesmo em 76 das 78 regiões metropolitanas brasileiras na comparação entre o segundo turno de 2022, quando Lula enfrentou Jair Bolsonaro (PL), e o segundo turno de 2026, em que disputou a reeleição contra Flávio Bolsonaro.

O petista reverteu o resultado apenas nas regiões metropolitanas de Maceió (AL) e Macapá (AP), onde Jair Bolsonaro havia vencido em 2022, mas em que Lula venceu Flávio Bolsonaro em 2026.

articles.title: Micro-ônibus pega fogo em rodovia do interior de SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Veículo estava sendo levado para manutenção quando as chamas começaram na Rodovia Comandante João Ribeiro de Barros (SP-294), entre Inúbia Paulista (SP) e Osvaldo Cruz (SP).
articles.summary: Um micro-ônibus escolar pegou fogo na Rodovia Comandante João Ribeiro de Barros (SP-294), entre Inúbia Paulista (SP) e Osvaldo Cruz (SP), na manhã desta quinta-feira (29).
articles.body:
Um micro-ônibus escolar pegou fogo na Rodovia Comandante João Ribeiro de Barros (SP-294), entre Inúbia Paulista (SP) e Osvaldo Cruz (SP), na manhã desta quinta-feira (29). Segundo a Prefeitura de Salmourão (SP), o veículo faz parte da frota municipal.

Conforme a concessionária que administra a rodovia, o veículo estava sendo levado para manutenção quando as chamas começaram no km 575, por volta das 9h45.

Motoristas que passavam pelo local registraram o momento em que uma fumaça preta saía do veículo. Assista ao vídeo acima.

Micro-ônibus escolar pega fogo em rodovia que liga Inúbia Paulista (SP) e Osvaldo Cruz (SP) — Foto: Reprodução/Folha Regional

Segundo as informações apuradas, o motorista trafegava por uma das faixas da rodovia quando percebeu a fumaça saindo do compartimento do motor.

Ele parou no acostamento para verificar o que estava acontecendo, mas, ao perceber o início das chamas, deixou o veículo por segurança. O fogo se alastrou rapidamente e foi controlado posteriormente pelas equipes de resgate.

Por causa da ocorrência, o trecho entre os quilômetros 574 e 575 precisou ser interditado. A pista foi liberada cerca de 1h30 depois, às 11h20 desta quinta-feira (29). Ninguém ficou ferido.

articles.title: Para aliados, Flávio esvazia liderança política ao apresentar dupla personalidade: moderado na campanha e extremista em carta | G1
articles.standfirst: Em carta divulgada nesta quarta-feira (28), Flávio voltou a não reconhecer o resultado das eleições e afirmou ser o "verdadeiro presidente do Brasil", o "presidente eleito".
articles.summary: Em carta divulgada nesta quarta-feira (28), Flávio voltou a não reconhecer o resultado das eleições e afirmou ser o "verdadeiro presidente do Brasil", o "presidente eleito".
articles.body:
Uma avaliação pragmática do núcleo mais próximo do senador e candidato derrotado Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) avalia que ele perdeu as credenciais políticas ao se alinhar em sua fuga do Brasil ao radicalismo de direita.

Nas palavras de um dos principais aliados de campanha, Flávio demonstrou uma espécie de dupla personalidade nessas últimas semanas : “Passou rapidamente de um candidato com perfil moderado para um extremista de direita com a divulgação da carta”.

Flávio desembarcou em Miami nesta quarta-feira (28), após deixar o Brasil e passar pela Argentina. O senador foi derrotado por Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) no segundo turno da eleição presidencial, realizado no domingo (25).

Há o reconhecimento que foi desastrosa a divulgação do texto em que ele se apresenta como “presidente eleito” do Brasil em uma das versões da carta. Os próprios aliados reconhecem mensagem de teor golpista de Flávio enfraqueceu a própria oposição.

Por isso mesmo, muitos líderes da direita começaram a se distanciar de Flávio e reconhecer a reeleição do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), como o governador Tarcísio de Freitas (SP) e o presidente do PL, partido de Flávio, Valdemar Costa Neto.

O ambiente na oposição é de perplexidade com Flávio não só pela carta, mas também pela fuga do Brasil e com a declaração no domingo negando a eleição de Lula .

“O tiro saiu pela culatra. Ao invés do discurso moderado da campanha, a percepção é que Flávio perdeu as credenciais para liderar a oposição ao governo Lula”, reforçou outro parlamentar bolsonarista.

Com isso, líderes da oposição passam a ter no discurso mais sóbrio de Tarcísio – de reconhecer a eleição de Lula e fazer uma oposição responsável – como principal referência para tentar atravessar esse período.

Já no governo, a ordem é não alimentar mais esse clima eleitoral que o Flávio tenta passar com a fuga . Nas palavras de um interlocutor de Lula, agora quem precisa reagir ao movimento golpista é o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral, o que já foi feito pelo presidente da Corte, ministro Kássio Nunes Marques .

Flávio Bolsonaro desembarca nos EUA — Foto: Eva Marie Uzcategui/Reuters

Em uma carta divulgada após fugir do Brasil rumo aos Estados Unidos, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) declarou nesta quarta-feira (28) não reconhecer o resultado das urnas no segundo turno da eleição presidencial, acusou suposta fraude eleitoral e afirmou ser o "verdadeiro presidente do Brasil", o "presidente eleito".

🔎 Após divulgar a primeira carta, em formato de imagens, em uma rede social, Flávio divulgou uma nova carta, também em imagens, em que substituiu as expressões "verdadeiro presidente do Brasil" e "presidente eleito" por "líder do Brasil" e "líder".

As alegações, divulgadas sem apresentação de provas, contrariam a postura do PL, partido de Flávio Bolsonaro , e contrastam com a confirmação da vitória de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) pelo Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE). O PL reconheceu o resultado eleitoral, pedindo esclarecimentos da Justiça.

No documento, Flávio agradeceu a líderes internacionais, como o presidente da Argentina, Javier Milei, e o presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, e afirmou que está em território norte-americano com a família e "em segurança".

O parlamentar atacou o Judiciário e alegou a existência de um "regime de exceção" e "perseguição política" contra a sua família, negando que sua saída represente uma fuga e comparando sua ida ao exterior a episódios de exílio político de figuras históricas.

articles.title: EUA pediram a Flávio Bolsonaro que retirasse de carta trecho em que se dizia ‘presidente eleito’ | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo assessores do Departamento de Estado dos Estados Unidos, expressão poderia dar a entender que o governo americano havia acolhido o senador nessa condição.
articles.summary: Segundo assessores do Departamento de Estado dos Estados Unidos, expressão poderia dar a entender que o governo americano havia acolhido o senador nessa condição.
articles.body:
O governo dos Estados Unidos pediu ao senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), candidato derrotado nas eleições presidenciais, que retirasse da carta divulgada por ele os trechos em que se apresentava como o “verdadeiro presidente eleito”.

Segundo assessores do Departamento de Estado dos Estados Unidos, a expressão poderia dar a entender que o governo americano havia acolhido o senador nessa condição , o que criaria problemas para as relações diplomáticas oficiais entre Brasil e Estados Unidos.

A informação foi divulgada pela colunista do UOL Mariana Sanches e confirmada pelo blog com diplomatas que acompanharam os acontecimentos de ontem.

Aliados de Flávio Bolsonaro afirmaram que a mudança foi apenas um ajuste no texto divulgado inicialmente ( entenda mais abaixo ).

Segundo os diplomatas ouvidos pelo blog , porém, a alteração ocorreu após uma posição do governo do presidente norte-americano Donald Trump ao tomar conhecimento do conteúdo da carta.

Trump autorizou a entrada de Flávio Bolsonaro no país e a concessão de visto humanitário a ele e à família.

Segundo assessores do Departamento de Estado, porém, aceitar a autodeclaração de Flávio Bolsonaro como presidente eleito poderia ser interpretado como um rompimento com o governo brasileiro.

Isso não está nos planos do governo Trump. Apesar de fazer críticas ao processo eleitoral brasileiro e levantar suspeitas sobre as eleições, Trump tem elogiado o presidente Lula e afirmado que gosta do petista.

Ou seja, uma coisa é receber Flávio Bolsonaro nos Estados Unidos. Outra seria acolhê-lo na condição de presidente eleito, o que não está nos planos do governo americano.

Primeira versão da carta postada por Flávio em uma rede social se chamava de 'presidente eleito' — Foto: Reprodução/X

Na primeira versão da carta divulgada nesta quarta (28), Flávio Bolsonaro se apresentou como o “verdadeiro presidente do Brasil” e “presidente eleito”, não reconheceu o resultado do segundo turno e alegou, sem apresentar provas, fraude na eleição.

Pouco depois, apagou a publicação e divulgou uma nova versão, na qual substituiu as expressões por “líder do Brasil” e “líder”.

Na carta, Flávio agradeceu aos presidentes dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, e da Argentina, Javier Milei, e afirmou estar em território americano com a família e “em segurança”.

O senador também disse que não fugiu do Brasil, alegou ser alvo de perseguição política e afirmou que passaria a liderar a oposição a partir dos Estados Unidos.

Flávio também questionou a decisão do ministro Cristiano Zanin , do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), que prorrogou em duas horas o período de votação no domingo (25).

A extensão do horário havia sido solicitada tanto pela coligação do presidente Lula quanto pela campanha do próprio Flávio, diante de problemas no transporte público de eleitores e de condições climáticas adversas.

Segundo o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), pouco mais de 34 mil votos foram registrados depois das 17h. Lula terminou a eleição com uma vantagem de 4,43 milhões de votos sobre Flávio.

O TSE confirmou a vitória de Lula e afirmou que a eleição transcorreu com segurança e transparência, sem fraudes ou inconsistências que comprometessem o resultado.

O próprio PL, partido de Flávio, reconheceu o resultado proclamado pelo TSE, embora tenha afirmado que os questionamentos levantados deveriam ser esclarecidos pela Justiça.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro: Governo não reagirá à fuga para EUA | G1
articles.standfirst: Avaliação nos bastidores é de que episódio não cria constrangimentos para o Brasil; Planalto pretende manter pragmatismo nas relações com Washington e Buenos Aires.
articles.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro fugiu do Brasil após questionar as urnas, mas o governo Lula manterá o pragmatismo com EUA e Argentina para evitar novas crises diplomáticas.
articles.body:
O governo brasileiro está convencido de que os Estados Unidos e a Argentina participaram da operação que permitiu a fuga do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) do Brasil, candidato derrotado à Presidência da República.

Apesar disso, o Palácio do Planalto não pretende se manifestar ou reagir diplomaticamente à atuação dos dois países. O governo entende que não há motivo para o presidente entrar diretamente na controvérsia. Uma eventual reação oficial dependerá do surgimento de novos fatos.

A avaliação é de que o episódio não cria constrangimento diplomático para o Brasil e não exige uma resposta oficial do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT).

A orientação é manter uma relação pragmática com os governos de Donald Trump e Javier Milei , sem permitir que isso interfira no diálogo diplomático e comercial.

O governo entende que o cenário atual é mais favorável que durante a crise do tarifaço, em, quando integrantes da família Bolsonaro atuaram junto ao governo norte-americano.

A avaliação é Lula chega à discussão fortalecido pela vitória nas urnas no último domingo (25), quando conquistou seu quarto mandato.

Integrantes do governo acreditam que o resultado das urnas enfraqueceu a articulação política de Flávio no exterior e reduziu o espaço para questionamentos sobre o processo eleitoral brasileiro.

Com os Estados Unidos, o governo pretende adotar a mesma estratégia utilizada durante a crise do tarifaço: manter o diálogo e evitar que divergências políticas prejudiquem os interesses dos países.

Outro fator considerado pelo governo brasileiro são as eleições legislativas americanas, marcadas para a próxima terça-feira. O governo entende que o resultado das chamadas eleições de meio de mandato será um "divisor de águas" para a relação entre Brasil e Estados Unidos.

A nova composição do Congresso americano, que poderá ter maioria de oposição na Câmara e no Senado, ajudará a definir a força política de Trump.

A diplomacia brasileira entende que será necessário aguardar o resultado das urnas americanas para avaliar com mais clareza o cenário político e os próximos passos da relação bilateral.

O ministro das Relações Exteriores, Mauro Vieira, viaja nesta quinta-feira (29) para Atlanta, onde participa de uma reunião de chanceleres do G20 na sexta-feira (30). O secretário de Estado americano, Marco Rubio, também estará no encontro.

Até o momento, não há reunião bilateral marcada entre os dois, mas o governo brasileiro não descarta uma conversa caso haja interesse por parte de Rubio.

A expectativa é de que Lula e Trump voltem a se encontrar durante a Cúpula do G20, prevista para dezembro, na Flórida.

Flávio Bolsonaro desembarca nos EUA — Foto: Eva Marie Uzcategui/Reuters

O governo brasileiro acredita que a gestão do presidente argentino Javier Milei também colaborou com a operação que permitiu a saída de Flávio Bolsonaro do Brasil. Mas, assim como em relação aos Estados Unidos, deve ser evitar uma reação caso não surja novos fatos.

O governo também acompanha a repercussão da carta divulgada por Flávio Bolsonaro após sua saída do Brasil.

Nos bastidores, a avaliação é de que o episódio expõe as dificuldades do senador após a derrota nas eleições presidenciais.

Integrantes do governo suspeitam que o conteúdo do documento possa ter passado por ajustes após contatos com autoridades americanas, por isso Flávio teria feito a mudança de "presidente eleito" para "líder".

Essa hipótese, no entanto, não foi confirmada pelo Departamento de Estado dos Estados Unidos.

A avaliação é de que a vitória eleitoral de Lula dá condições políticas para seguir com a agenda sem transformar as movimentações de Flávio Bolsonaro em um novo foco de tensão com os Estados Unidos e a Argentina.

articles.title: Rui Costa questiona articulação que prevê anistia a Jair Bolsonaro | G1
articles.standfirst: Ex-ministro e senador eleito pela Bahia, aliado do presidente Lula (PT) defende que tema não deve ser central do governo federal, nem do Congresso. "Nós devemos falar mais de povo", defende.
articles.summary: Ex-ministro e senador eleito pela Bahia, aliado do presidente Lula (PT) defende que tema não deve ser central do governo, nem do Congresso. "Nós devemos falar mais de povo", disse.
articles.body:
Rui Costa, ministro-chefe da Casa Civil, ao lado do Presidente da República, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), participa da cerimônia de assinatura do contrato de concessão da BR-381/MG, no Palácio do Planalto, em Brasília (DF), em 22 de janeiro de 2025. — Foto: Fátima Meira/Enquadrar/Estadão Conteúdo

Senador eleito e ex-ministro do governo Lula 3, Rui Costa (PT-BA) questionou a articulação feita no Senado a favor da reeleição de Davi Alcolumbre (União Brasil-AP) à presidência do Senado.

O debate prevê conceder anistia ou um indulto ao ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL), condenado a 27 anos e 3 meses de prisão no julgamento da trama golpista no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) - ele cumpre prisão domiciliar por questões de saúde.

Rui Costa disse que não está acompanhando a negociação, mas considera que a escolha do presidente do Senado tenha que passar por "intromissão com as penas das pessoas", sejam as condenadas na trama golpista, sejam as condenadas no 8 de Janeiro.

"Eu sou a favor do distensionamento político, que a gente não coloque essa questão da polarização política no centro do governo, nem do Congresso Nacional", disse. "A gente deve tirar da agenda essa centralidade na polarização e, eventualmente, na discussão dos crimes cometidos por qualquer família, inclusive a família Bolsonaro".

Segundo o senador, esta não deve ser a agenda do país para os próximos quatro anos. Ele alertou que os políticos devem olhar para o que disseram os resultados das urnas em 25 de outubro.

"Essa multidão que foi nas ruas está preocupada com o que é que nós políticos, senadores, deputados, governo executivo, o que é que nós vamos fazer para melhorar a vida cotidiana deles", afirmou.

Ele exemplificou dizendo que quem pega ônibus, quem precisa de segurança e outros temas querem que o governo tenha que "apontar soluções, apontar caminhos". "Nós devemos falar mais de povo, falar mais da vida das pessoas".

O Blog da Sadi informou nesta quinta-feira (29) que Davi Alcolumbre articula um acordo para conter o impeachment de ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) . Além disso, ele admite discutir um indulto e uma anistia a Jair Bolsonaro em busca da reeleição como presidente do Senado em 2027.

O foco é o componente de sobrevivência política nessa movimentação: a tentativa de construir um acordo que viabilize sua reeleição à presidência do Senado.

O indulto, ou seja, o perdão judicial, é competência do presidente da República, de acordo com a Constituição. Já a anistia depende do Congresso Nacional.

A avaliação feita por esses interlocutores é que, caso Alcolumbre consiga uma aproximação com o grupo de Bolsonaro, sua situação na disputa pelo comando da Casa muda significativamente.

articles.standfirst: Na segunda (26), o presidente do Supremo já havia determinado o arquivamento de outras três investigações, que miravam o pastor Silas Malafaia, o jornalista e escritor Guilherme Fiuza e o ex-deputado Eduardo Bolsonaro.
articles.summary: Na segunda (26), o presidente do Supremo já havia determinado o arquivamento de outras três investigações, que miravam o pastor Silas Malafaia, o jornalista e escritor Guilherme Fiuza e o ex-deputado Eduardo Bolsonaro.
articles.body:
Ministro Edson Fachin — Foto: Reprodução

O presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), ministro Edson Fachin , determinou o arquivamento de cinco investigações que surgiram a partir do inquérito das Fake News.

🔎O inquérito é uma investigação aberta pelo STF em 2019 para apurar a existência de notícias fraudulentas, falsas comunicações de crimes, denúncias caluniosas, ameaças e outros ataques contra o STF, seus ministros e familiares.

As decisões foram assinadas na quarta (28), mas foram divulgadas apenas nesta quinta (29).

Com isso, inquéritos, petições e demais procedimentos que ainda não resultaram em denúncia passaram a depender de decisão da presidência do STF.

Nesta quarta, o presidente determinou o arquivamento de cinco investigações que apuravam:

➡️publicações do Partido da Causa Operária (PCO) com críticas ao STF nas redes sociais;

➡️postagens contendo apologia a crimes de racismo contra judeus e contra a vida de ministros do STF, divulgada em grupo do aplicativo Telegram;

➡️suposta divulgação, por parte de Flávia Cordeiro Magalhães, também identificada como Flávia Magalhães Soares, de notícias fraudulentas sobre a atuação do STF e de um dos ministros;

➡️da possível atuação de Gilson Machado Guimarães Neto, ex-ministro do Turismo, perante o Consulado de Portugal em Recife (PE), para viabilizar a emissão de passaporte português, com objetivo de permitir a saída do território nacional de Mauro César Barbosa Cid, delator da trama golpista;

➡️uso de redes sociais “com o objetivo de prejudicar a normalidade das eleições presidenciais de 2022, em um contexto de incentivo à recusa dos resultados e de defesa de ruptura institucional”, promovida pelo deputado estadual Alex Brasil.

Segundo o STF, a determinação atende a manifestações da Procuradoria-geral da República (PGR), que identificou a falta de provas em alguns casos, e a prescrição de outros.

Na segunda (26), o presidente do Supremo já havia determinado o arquivamento de outras três investigações relacionadas ao inquérito das Fake News, que miravam o pastor Silas Malafaia, o jornalista e escritor Guilherme Fiuza e o ex-deputado Eduardo Bolsonaro.

No caso do filho do ex-presidente, no entanto, o inquérito já havia se tornado uma ação penal e ele acabou condenado pelo crime de coação no curso do processo.

Fachin entendeu que o pedido de apurações já havia cumprido a finalidade para a qual foi instaurado.

articles.title: Israel election: Partial results indicate possible deadlock, Netanyahu alleges fraud
articles.summary: Both main coalitions are projected to fall short of a parliamentary majority.
articles.body:
Israeli election authorities were still counting votes from Tuesday's parliamentary election on Thursday morning.

But even with the vast majority of ballots counted, it remained unclear who will form the country's new government. Neither the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor that of his prime challenger Gadi Eisenkot has an obvious course to secure a majority of seats in the Knesset, according to exit polls and partial results released by electoral authorities.

As of Thursday, Israel's Central Election Committee said it had counted nearly 94% of votes. The partial results -- which are subject to some change as the rest of the votes are tallied -- indicated that Netanyahu's Likud party would win 26 seats, with Eisenkot's Yashar party on 21 seats.

The CEC projected that Netanyahu's coalition was on course to secure 53 seats, slightly ahead of Eisenkot's bloc on 48 seats. Neither coalition was on course to achieve a 61-seat majority.

The Arab parties, meanwhile, were projected by the CEC to take 19 seats.

The last stage of vote counting is expected to end on Thursday afternoon or evening local time, the CEC said. The final results will not be published until Nov. 4.

If the CEC projections hold true, the two coalitions led by Netanyahu and Eisenkot may need the backing of the Arab-Israeli parties to have any chance of a majority in the Knesset.

Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have previously ruled out forming a coalition with the Arab parties. In his post-election speech, Netanyahu suggested that any government that included Arab parties would "endanger Israel."

Arab party leaders have indicated willingness to work with the anti-Netanyahu opposition. The Arab-led Joint List -- a collection of three parties which between them were on course to win 12 seats as of Wednesday -- said in a statement that they were ready for "political cooperation to oust the Netanyahu government."

"The Joint List will work with all its strength to bring an end to Netanyahu's rule. We are ready for political cooperation to establish an alternative government, which will present a true alternative and commit itself to a true change of the current government's racist policy," it said in a statement.

Mansour Abbas, the leader of the United Arab List -- also known as Ra'am -- which was projected to win seven seats, said he had been in touch with representatives of both the Netanyahu and Eisenkot coalitions.

As vote counting continued on Wednesday, Netanyahu alleged -- without providing any evidence -- that the election had been "stolen by Arab parties," claiming that Likud had gathered evidence of electoral fraud and submitted it to electoral, law enforcement and security bodies.

Likud issued a statement claiming that "foreign entities" had interfered with the election by providing financial support to Arab parties. The party did not immediately provide any evidence to support its allegation.

Opposition leaders condemned the prime minister's remarks, maintaining that the elections in Israel were free and fair and there was no evidence of election fraud. The Israeli police said they will investigate any credible allegations of wrongdoing.

Dean Livne, the acting director general of the CEC said on Wednesday that there was "no basis for allegations of election theft," as reported by Israel's Kan radio station.

Eisenkot, meanwhile, said on Wednesday night that he had undertaken "a long day of meetings, conversations, and preparations to realize the will of the voter."

"We are focused on the heavy task entrusted to us -- bringing change to Israel," he wrote in a post to X.

ABC News' Nasser Atta and Joe Simonetti contributed to this report.

articles.title: Report: Obama Admin Uncovered Evidence Against Omar's Marriage
articles.summary: Report: Obama Admin Uncovered Evidence Against Omar's Marriage
articles.body:
Federal investigators found evidence during the Obama administration suggesting that Rep. Ilhan Omar's 2009 marriage to a man suspected of being her brother was intended to help him obtain a green card, but the case stalled chiefly because prosecutors concluded the suspected offense fell outside a five-year statute of limitations, according to a new report.

The FBI and Department of Homeland Security investigated the marriage in the summer of 2016, current and former officials told The New York Times in a report published Thursday.

The officials' account challenges Omar's characterization of the earlier inquiry as having debunked allegations that she married her brother to help him obtain a green card.

The newspaper said it remains unclear what evidence investigators had establishing that Omar and her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, are siblings.

Marrying a person to help them obtain a green card is illegal under federal law, while marrying a sibling is illegal under state law.

However, the newspaper noted that it remains unclear whether federal prosecutors could pursue charges against Omar despite the statute of limitations for marriage-based immigration fraud.

Omar has repeatedly denied the allegations about her and her ex-husband.

"Rep. Omar has repeatedly and unequivocally denied this baseless, disgusting conspiracy theory," spokeswoman Jackie Rogers said in a statement. "This is a desperate political smear designed to distract from Trump's failed presidency and two years of Republican failure in Congress."

Six current and former officials familiar with the 2016 investigation told the Times that agents found evidence suggesting Omar and Elmi were siblings. The officials said investigators had limited tools to develop the case because prosecutors did not pursue it.

Omar was already a U.S. citizen when she married Elmi, a British citizen, in 2009. They divorced in 2017.

Two former officials said Elmi obtained a conditional two-year green card through the marriage. When immigration authorities requested additional evidence before granting him permanent status without conditions, he left the United States and abandoned his petition, they said.

The earlier inquiry involved an FBI agent specializing in public corruption and civil rights cases and two Homeland Security Investigations agents, according to the report.

The allegations surfaced publicly in 2016 as Omar campaigned for a seat in the Minnesota House of Representatives. After a local television station reported that the U.S. attorney's office had opened an investigation, her campaign sought a letter from Andrew Luger, then the U.S. attorney for Minnesota.

In the Aug. 22, 2016, letter, Luger wrote that "my office is not investigating, nor have we requested an investigation into Ms. Omar."

Omar portrayed the letter as an exoneration that put to rest "flat-out falsehoods."

Luger, however, told the Times last week that the letter "was never meant to say anything about the substance of the claims." He said it was intended only to rebut an erroneous report that he had asked ICE to investigate Omar.

Luger said federal agents could have been pursuing the matter without his knowledge and denied shielding Omar from scrutiny.

The Trump administration has reopened scrutiny of the marriage as part of a broader investigation into the Omar family's immigration history. Federal agents searched the congresswoman's Washington home Oct. 12, weeks before she seeks a fifth term in the House.

Investigators are also examining whether Omar's late father submitted false or incomplete information during the immigration process and whether Omar was too old to qualify for citizenship through him in 2000, the Times reported.

Democrats have condemned the inquiry as political persecution and said the search violated Justice Department policy intended to prevent investigative actions from influencing elections.

President Donald Trump repeated the allegation that Omar married her brother last week. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the broader investigation could lead to Omar's deportation if authorities establish that she should not have been admitted to the country.

articles.title: Judge strikes down Trump admin's definition of 'medically frail' in Medicaid work rules
articles.summary: The guidance released in June "is beyond the powers of CMS and thus contrary to law," the federal judge in Boston said.
articles.body:
A federal judge in Boston sided on Thursday with a coalition of 25 Democratic-led states and the District of Columbia in a lawsuit challenging the Trump administration's requirement that states force chronically ill people on Medicaid to prove they are unable to work .

During oral arguments last week, the states said that unless the court blocked that piece of the rule before January and allowed them to exempt people with certain diagnosed illnesses, they would be "forced… to bear the costs and burdens of operationalizing this unlawful limitation."

Judge Richard Stearns, an appointee of President Bill Clinton, said the guidance the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services released in June went beyond what Congress passed in 2025 in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act , and is "thus contrary to law."

"There is an inherent public interest in ensuring that the government follows the law," he said, adding that "enforcement of an unlawful definition of 'medically frail' may lead to the disenrollment of otherwise eligible vulnerable individuals relying on Medicaid coverage for continuity of care."

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act mandated that people who receive Medicaid through the expansion of the program created in the Affordable Care Act — typically low-income people without young children — must work, volunteer or go to school for 80 hours a month to keep their benefits. But it exempted people too medically frail to work.

The court also ordered states to hold off for at least six months after the work rules take effect before they cancel the health insurance of anyone claiming a medical exemption to give them time to update their verification systems to comply with the ruling.

The ruling blocks only the "medical frailty" portion of the law and leaves the rest of the Medicaid work requirements, which will be enforced nationally beginning in January, in place.

CMS declined to comment on the decision and whether they plan to appeal it.

The ruling follows months of turmoil around the country as states raced to implement the Medicaid work requirements before the January deadline. Doctors, hospitals, community health centers and patient advocacy groups have been raising alarms about the burden placed on them by the Trump administration's medical frailty rule — arguing they will be forced to spend time and resources they don't have on the what they view as the often impossible task of evaluating chronically ill patients' ability to work.

"We're trained to do preventive care and help people navigate their illnesses. We're not trained to decide whether someone is able to work," Eva Shapiro, a physician in Tucson, Arizona, told reporters on a press call about the rules last week. "Patients with chronic conditions may have good weeks and bad weeks, and even those who are working may have difficulty navigating additional paperwork and reporting requirements."

Stearns reject challenges from the states to other aspects of the law. The judge, for instance, sided with the government on a requirement that states reject proof of patients' medical frailty — like a hospital admission or diagnosis — that is more than 12 months old.

States argued the provision will lead to greater disenrollments because sometimes a frail individual will go longer than 12 months between major health services.

The judge ruled that CMS provided a rationale for that "lookback" provision and therefore it was not arbitrary as the states contended.

"That the states (or even the court) may disagree with the wisdom of the agency's policies and conclusions, or may have made different choices, is irrelevant," he wrote.

Stearns also sided with the Trump administration on its policy letting states decide whether or not to accept a patient's pledge that they are too sick to work in lieu of proof for the first year the work requirement is in effect.

Starting in 2028, Medicaid expansion enrollees nationwide can self-attest once but then during their next renewal they must prove that their condition prevents them from working.

Eight states have rejected the one year grace period and will require that paperwork in 2027, arguing that allowing patients to "self-attest" could lead to fraudulent enrollments.

The states' case argued that the Trump administration should have required all states to accept self-attestation of medical frailty.

Another lawsuit challenging the policy, filed by medical groups and the city of Columbus, Ohio, remains pending in a Maryland federal court.
authors: Alice Miranda Ollstein and Robert King

articles.title: New Texas Senate poll shows challenge for GOP in final days
articles.summary: A new poll shows Republicans in a tighter Texas Senate race than usual as early voting ends, with Paxton’s support lagging Talarico’s. See the numbers.
articles.body:
A new poll of Texas' U.S. Senate race is the latest to show Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton separated by just a few points, with early voting ending Friday

A new poll from Texas Southern University released Oct. 29 found that Talarico leads Paxton by 2 percentage points, 49% to 47%, with 3% supporting Libertarian Ted Brown and 1% undecided.

The poll was conducted before President Donald Trump 's two stops in Texas earlier in the week, where he campaigned for Paxton in Corpus Christi and Lubbock — where Talarico also held a campaign rally a few miles away.

Here's what the latest poll shows and how it compares with other recent polls since early voting began.

James Talarico, Ken Paxton statistically tied in Texas Senate race

The Texas Southern University poll surveyed 2,000 Texans likely to vote in the November 2026 general election between Oct. 21-25.

With a margin of error of 2.19 percentage points, Talarico's two-point edge is a statistical tie.

The poll also found that 48% of likely voters view Talarico favorably and 51% unfavorably, while 42% view Paxton favorably and 57% unfavorably.

By party, 99% of Democrats intend to vote for Talarico, 1% for Paxton and none for Brown or undecided.

For Republicans, 88% said they intend to vote for Paxton, with 8% intending to vote for Talarico, 3% for Brown and 1% still undecided.

Talarico led among independents, with 54% saying they would vote for Talarico, 38% for Paxton, 6% for Brown and 2% undecided.

Latest Talarico-Paxton Texas Senate race polls

Over the past few months, Democrat Talarico has led or tied Paxton either within the margin of error — making it a statistical tie — or just outside it.

A new Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media poll, released Oct. 22, found that 48% of likely voters support Talarico and 46% support Paxton — a 2-point lead within the poll's 3.1 percentage points margin of error.

The Cook Political Report also published a battleground poll, released Oct. 21, on the Texas Senate race showing Talarico leading Republican Paxton 49% to 44% — a 5-point lead outside the poll's 3.2 percentage points margin of error.

Here's how they compare with other recent October polls:

U of H Hobby poll (Oct. 18) — Talarico 48%, Paxton 46%.

Marist poll (Oct. 14) — Talarico 47%, Paxton 45%.

UT/Texas Politics Project (Oct. 13) — Talarico 50%, Paxton 47%.

ReconMR (Oct. 13) — Talarico 48%, Paxton 44%.

UMass Lowell (Oct. 8) — Talarico 45%, Paxton 45%.

YouGov poll (Oct. 6) — Talarico 50%, Paxton 44%.

The New York Times (Oct. 3) — Talarico 51%, Paxton 45%.

Mateo Rosiles is the Texas Connect reporter for USA TODAY and its regional papers in Texas, based in Austin. Got a news tip for him? Email him at mrosiles@usatodayco.com .

articles.title: 'Decoy Dan' Sullivan case leads top senator to break four-year X silence: 'Pattern of Lies'
articles.summary: Lisa Murkowski broke years of silence on X to accuse Mary Peltola's team of ballot manipulation through a decoy Dan Sullivan candidate scheme.
articles.body:
The reported recruitment by Democrats of a second "Dan Sullivan" to allegedly confuse voters in Alaska's Senate race drew a rare public rebuke from Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, who appeared to break four years of silence on her personal X account.

The New York Times reported that members of Mary Peltola's team helped recruit a candidate who shares the name of incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, potentially confusing voters in a closely watched race that also features Republican Gerald Heikes.

In a statement on her personal account @LisaForSenate , Murkowski said the report "revealed… a pattern of lies and coverups" on the part of Peltola.

"While some may try to write this off as just how politics works now, ballot-stacking should have no place in our electoral process," Murkowski said.

"Run and win on your merits: your views, your policy ideas, and your accomplishments. By contrast, recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong."

"Alaskans deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign," she said, adding that such a "culture of deception" does not belong in elections or with lawmakers.

Her previous post on the account was dated November 2022 and featured a video message wishing Alaskans a happy Thanksgiving.

Murkowski's official Senate account posts regularly, with its two most recent posts criticizing the Trump Justice Department for launching a lawsuit in the "Decoy Dan" situation prior to the Times' report and highlighting her visit to the Alaska Federation of Natives Convention.

The Times reported this week that the effort extended beyond recruiting the second Sullivan, with Democratic operatives also seeking other candidates who could siphon votes from the Republican incumbent.

The second "decoy" Sullivan , reportedly a longtime registered nonpartisan, lives in the remote community of Petersburg.

Sullivan told Fox News that the scheme is what arises when a "far left" candidate "has got nothing to run on."

Fox News Digital reached out to Murkowski for further comment.

While the post marked Murkowski's first intervention on X in Alaska's election contests, the Republican recently drew attention by endorsing Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins over three Republicans: Bernadette Wilson, Treg Taylor and Dave Bronson.

Murkowski's father, former Sen. Frank Murkowski, joined his daughter in that announcement.

The split Republican field positions Kreiss-Tomkins as the mathematical favorite, according to the Alaska Beacon.

Murkowski was also a champion of the ranked-choice system that produced four-person general election ballots.

Murkowski's pointed criticism of Peltola puts fresh scrutiny on the reported recruitment effort and what the Democrat's campaign knew as voters prepare to cast their ballots.

articles.title: Bari Weiss faced 'significant resistance' from CBS News staffers about Alaska ballot scandal, insiders say
articles.summary: CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss faced resistance among staff at a meeting when talking about the New York Times' report on the Alaska ballot scandal.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE — CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss faced "significant resistance" from staff at Thursday's 9 a.m. meeting about the growing Alaska ballot controversy, network insiders told Fox News Digital. "This is a scandal," Weiss declared to staff. According to multiple sources on the call, several CBS News staffers pushed back at Weiss' enthusiasm over the bombshell New York Times report alleging Democrats schemed to find a Dan Sullivan to run against incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, in hopes of aiding Democratic opponent Mary Peltola. DEM STRATEGIST SHRUGS OFF ALASKA BALLOT SCANDAL ON MS NOW, INSISTS 'THIS STUFF HAPPENS ALL THE TIME' Many on the call shrugged it off as routine politics and said Republicans have also engaged in similar scheming. When Weiss asked for other examples of ballot confusion, "Face the Nation" moderator Margaret Brennan pointed to New Hampshire Senate candidate John Sununu, suggesting that midterm voters might confuse him with his brother, former New Hampshire Gov. Chris Sununu. ALASKA'S GOVERNOR ORDERS INVESTIGATION AFTER NYT REPORT ON ALLEGED DEM-LINKED SENATE ELECTION SCHEME CBS News political correspondent Ed O'Keefe also insisted that such tactics are nothing new. Earlier that morning, during his appearance on "CBS Mornings," O'Keefe stressed to viewers that what happened in Alaska "could be a dirty trick, but it's not illegal," adding that "this has happened before, kind of." He pointed to the 2016 Alaska Senate race when former Anchorage mayor Dan Sullivan — no relation to the U.S. Senator of the same name — briefly ran against incumbent Sen. Lisa Murkowski in the GOP primary, hoping "name recognition" of the other sitting senator would help his own candidacy. A separate CBS staffer on the call pushed back against the notion that colleagues like Brennan and O'Keefe were trying to downplay the scandal, telling Fox News Digital they were providing context to the story being discussed. MARY PELTOLA'S CAMPAIGN, DEMS BACKED COVERT SCHEME TO FIELD SPOILER CANDIDATES IN ALASKA SENATE RACE: REPORT The staffer also said the meeting was never contentious and that it was a "healthy, good conversation." Still, Weiss called the uproar in Alaska a "great story" that the network should follow and urged staff to push for stories like the one The New York Times broke, calling it a "learning moment." Some staffers who attended the meeting virtually were either en route or on the ground in Alaska to provide updates on their own reporting after being directed there Wednesday night, including CBS News congressional reporter Taurean Small. A spokesperson for CBS News declined to comment. Republicans have long been suspicious about the candidacy of Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher who is among four Senate candidates listed on Alaska's rank-choice ballot. The Department of Justice filed a lawsuit against the state of Alaska seeking to block certification of the election results if the incumbent senator loses and votes cast for the other Sullivan could have changed the outcome. On Wednesday, The New York Times alleged his candidacy was no coincidence. "In the summer of 2025, a staffer for Mary Peltola, the Alaska Democrat who was eyeing a run for Senate, received unusual instructions from top campaign aides: Find as many people named Dan Sullivan in Alaska as you can," the Times began its report Wednesday. "The staffer complied, combing through voter records to produce a list of Dan Sullivans from across the state. ... [I]f the Peltola campaign or its allies could track down and persuade another Dan Sullivan to run for Senate, the confusion could cost the senator crucial votes on the state’s unusual, four-person ballot. The plan worked," the report said. SEN DAN SULLIVAN BRANDS PELTOLA'S ALLEGED BALLOT SCHEME A 'SCANDAL AT THE HIGHEST ORDER' According to Peltola's former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, Peltola was not directly involved in the scheme but was "definitely aware." Peltola's campaign has denied involvement in his candidacy. "But The Times has found, based on interviews and text messages, along with documents prepared for a potential lawsuit against the campaign, that not only did Ms. Peltola’s team work with people trying to recruit Mr. Sullivan to run for Senate, but the effort was much broader," the Times reported. "The group worked to coax other would-be spoilers into the race, to dilute the incumbent’s support and help catapult the Democrat to victory." Peltola called the Times report a "distraction" and "stuff to sell newspapers." However, Republican Alaska Gov. articles.title: Platner drops f-bomb after being tracked down by reporter in Maine
articles.summary: Disgraced former Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner dropped an f-bomb in response to questions from a New York Post reporter who tracked him down in his remote oceanside community in Maine. “Who the f‑‑‑ are you weirdos?” Platner asked a reporter while pulling a kayak from the water. The reporter asked what Platner had been…
articles.body:
Disgraced former Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner dropped an f-bomb in response to questions from a New York Post reporter who tracked him down in his remote oceanside community in Maine.

“Who the f‑‑‑ are you weirdos?” Platner asked a reporter while pulling a kayak from the water.

The reporter asked what Platner had been up to since exiting the Maine Senate race amid claims of sexual assault by an ex-girlfriend. Platner was ultimately replaced by state Sen. Troy Jackson (D).

“What the f‑‑‑ does it look like I’m up to? I’m being an oyster farmer,” Platner yelled at a reporter. “It just seems to be, like, life, man.”

Steven Vago, the reporter, said the exchange occurred in Sullivan, Maine, where Platner was an oyster farmer before and after his insurgent Senate campaign.

“How’s that going,” Vago asks of oyster farming.

“Well it goes the way it always goes, friend,” Platner responds.

“What does that mean?” the reporter says.

“It means the people from away have no idea what it is we do for a living,” Platner says.

The former candidate didn’t respond to a question about his prediction for Tuesday, when the Maine Senate race will be among the most closely watched in the country.

A CNN/SSRS poll reported Jackson up by 4 points against Sen. Susan Collins (R). The poll also found about 9 in 10 likely voters in Maine said they are locked into their choice.

Platner stayed in the race despite a string of scandals, including past Reddit comments that embraced communism, insulted police and appeared to put some blame on intoxicated victims of sexual assault.

But the testimony of a former girlfriend, first published in Politico, finally pushed him out of the race, coming after previous reports of problematic behavior with former romantic partners. Jenny Racicot, 41, said Platner forced her to have sex with him despite her repeated objections.

Another woman who dated him on and off for several years alleged to The Washington Post that Platner removed condoms without her consent while they were having sex.

Jackson is slightly favored to defeat Collins — the only Republican running for reelection this cycle in a state that former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024 — according to Decision Desk HQ .

articles.title: Vance makes fiery closing pitch for Paxton: ‘Texas is not surrendering a damn thing’
articles.summary: WEATHERFORD, Texas — Vice President delivered a fiery closing pitch for Republican Senate candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton on Thursday, telling supporters the Lone Star State would not surrender “a damn thing” on Election Day. “I need you to send a message on November the 3rd that America belongs to those who love…
articles.body:
WEATHERFORD, Texas — Vice President delivered a fiery closing pitch for Republican Senate candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton on Thursday, telling supporters the Lone Star State would not surrender “a damn thing” on Election Day.

“I need you to send a message on November the 3rd that America belongs to those who love it, not those who hate,” Vance exclaimed to a large crowd of supporters in North Texas.

“I need you to tell James Talarico that this weird obsession with trans kids is not good for the state of Texas, and I need you to send the message to every far-left activist, to everybody who expects Texas to surrender, that in five days Texas is not surrendering a damn thing,” he continued of the Democratic state lawmaker challenging Paxton for the Senate seat.

The vice president received a warm welcome from hundreds of supporters at a construction facility roughly 30 miles west of Fort Worth, with supporters changing “JD” as he took to the stage. There was a sizable overflow crowd of supporters watching on a jumbotron outside of the main event space.

Vance took a number of jabs at Talarico on cultural issues, including masculinity and trans athletes in women’s sports.

The vice president also sought to attack Talarico over gas prices, an area where Republicans have struggled with their messaging amid the U.S. war in Iran, which has driven up energy costs.

“It takes a certain kind of audacity for Democrats like James Talarico to say that Texas energy jobs are immoral, which is what he has said, and then to run talking about the price of gas,” Vance said.

“Right here in Texas, we can make more of our own energy, drill more of our own energy,” he added.

Vance also announced that the Department of Agriculture is opening a new beef processing facility in Texas, crediting Paxton and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins.

“Because thanks to Ken’s advocacy and thanks, importantly, to Brooke Rollins’s hustle, the Department of Agriculture is devoting millions to the opening of a new beef processing facility right here in Texas,” he told supporters.

The vice president previously campaigned in Tyler, Texas, earlier this month. Vance and President Trump have made a number of trips to the state to boost Paxton, who has trailed Talarico in several recent polls.

A CNN poll released on Thursday showed Paxton trailing Talarico 49 percent to 43 percent among registered Texas voters.

articles.title: Dem probes could ‘torture’ young Trump officials with crushing legal bills, subpoenaed conservative warns
articles.summary: Rachel Bovard of CPI warns Democrats could follow Jack Smith's playbook to target young Trump administration officials with costly subpoenas.
articles.body: Repeated calls by Democratic lawmakers to investigate President Donald Trump and his allies are raising concerns from a conservative organization previously subpoenaed during former Biden-appointed special counsel Jack Smith’s 2020 election investigation. And one of its leaders is warning that young professionals could face reputational damage and steep legal bills. Rachel Bovard, vice president of programs at the Conservative Partnership Institute (CPI), said Smith's investigation left her organization on the hook for millions of dollars in fees to ensure compliance with the subpoenas. HOUSE DEMS PLOT TRUMP INVESTIGATION BLITZ IF THEY SEIZE MAJORITY "Jack Smith was a test run in how to do this," Bovard told Fox News Digital. "Jack Smith basically went in crazy, subpoenaed a host of information across the right. His goal was to map the right, and he did it. And all of that information is still on file at the FBI and the Justice Department. It doesn't go away, so it's sitting there waiting for the next Dem administration to pick it up, and we expect that's what they'll do with it." Though CPI was targeted by the Biden Justice Department and not Congress, Bovard said she fears Democrats will follow what she described as Smith's playbook if they win control of Congress in the midterm elections. The concerns come after Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., stated during an event earlier this month at the University of Chicago's Institute of Politics that she wants Democrats to send a "deterrence message" to any young person considering working in the Trump administration. Slotkin said she wants to "not just focus on the president, but on the people who enabled him." "They literally just want to use the government as a political weapon, which is exactly what Jack Smith also did to a bunch of people, including my organization," Bovard told Fox News Digital. "We were never credibly accused of any crime, but we had to spend millions of dollars to comply with subpoenas." Bovard said Smith's subpoenas allowed the Justice Department to obtain detailed information such as CPI's health coverage and benefits, which she said had no relevance to Smith's investigation. Fox News Digital reached out to Slotkin's office for comment but did not receive a response before publication. Abhishek Kambli, a former federal prosecutor and a partner at Holtzman Vogel, told Fox News Digital that Congress' ability to issue subpoenas and conduct investigations must be related to legislative duties and that Congress can't issue subpoenas for law enforcement purposes. Kambli said remarks by Slotkin and other members of Congress could be used as evidence by anyone seeking to challenge a subpoena. "You had multiple members of the House and the Senate that talk about the accountability agenda and holding the Trump administration accountable for wrongdoing," Kambli told Fox News Digital. "And if they just throw in boilerplate language that this is for legislative purpose, anyone challenging those subpoenas will have that entire record to demonstrate that it's anything but that." While Michael Morley, a law professor at Florida State University College of Law, agreed that Slotkin's remarks are bad optics, he said Congress' authority to conduct investigations is still broad, pointing out that Congress can investigate the agencies it has created. "I don't think that is consistent with our norms, and I certainly don't think it's something that we'd like to see become a routine part of our discourse," Morley said of Slotkin's remarks. "But I don't think that necessarily means it rises to the level of a constitutional issue." ELISSA SLOTKIN CALLS BACKLASH TO THREAT OF PROSECUTION COMMENTS 'MANUFACTURED OUTRAGE' Hans von Spakovsky, a senior legal fellow at Advancing American Freedom, said that while Congress may be able to hold someone in criminal contempt for not complying with a subpoena, it's up to the Justice Department to prosecute, which it could decline to do. Spakovsky said that precedent was established during the Obama administration, when the Justice Department declined to prosecute then-Attorney General Eric Holder after the House held him in contempt for refusing to comply with a subpoena related to the Fast and Furious investigation. But Kambli said that doesn't erase the risks potential Trump administration officials could face, arguing that the investigative process itself can be the punishment. "There is no doubt that some members of Congress intend to use that process to bankrupt people who cannot afford legal representation," Kambli told Fox News Digital. "That is a real threat, regardless of whether anyone is ultimately prosecuted." SLOTKIN'S VIRAL 'THREAT' TO CONSERVATIVES TAKES NEW TWIST AS STUDENT MOVES TO HOLD HER ACCOUNTABLE: 'SHOCKING' Bovard said when she first saw Slotkin's remarks about seeking a "deterrence message" she interpreted them as a call to use the investigative process to "torture" young professionals. "I don't know that these Democrats think they can actually put people in jail. I think that's almost beside the point for them," Bovard told Fox News Digital. Kambli said concerns remain that if a Democrat returns to the White House, former Trump administration officials could be subjected to Justice Department investigations. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Where the real exposure lies is in the scenario where a Democrat wins the presidency in 2028, and they maintain both houses of Congress," Kambli told Fox News Digital. Just weeks before Slotkin's remarks, Trump said during an interview with Time magazine that he would issue preemptive pardons to members of his administration before leaving the White House, pointing out that President Joe Biden issued a pardon for Dr. Anthony Fauci. Bovard said it was unfortunate that political affairs had reached a point where mass pardons were even under consideration, but she argued they made sense given the rise in lawfare. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "This is how we're going to have to live: mass pardons of your political parties on either side, and that's obviously a terrible outcome. But if, you know, the Slotkin theory is put to the test. I don't think Trump's going to have a choice. I think he's going to have to do that," Bovard told Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Trump hammers culture war attacks on Andrews in final rally for Graham
articles.summary: President Trump launched a barrage of culture war attacks Thursday against Democratic Senate nominee Annie Andrews during his third and final campaign rally for Sen. Darline Graham (R) in South Carolina. “Darline Graham has devoted her entire life to the people of this state, and now she’s running to save you from a radical left…
articles.body:
President Trump launched a barrage of culture war attacks Thursday against Democratic Senate nominee Annie Andrews during his third and final campaign rally for Sen. Darline Graham (R) in South Carolina.

“Darline Graham has devoted her entire life to the people of this state, and now she’s running to save you from a radical left lunatic,” Trump said to the crowd before using an anti-transgender slur he’s often applied to the career pediatrician’s name.

He also called Andrews a “mutilizer, a rabid advocate for taxpayer-funded child sexual mutilation.”

Andrews, in a direct-to-camera ad earlier this month, hit back on the allegations from Trump.

“So I want you to hear me loud and clear: I don’t support biological men playing women’s sports and I don’t support — and haven’t ever performed — gender surgery for minors,” Andrews says in the ad.

The physician has in the past supported gender-affirming care for transgender youth. In 2022, she opposed the Save Women’s Sports act in South Carolina that would ban transgender students from participating in school sports that align with their gender identity, calling it a “shameful legislation that does nothing to protect or support women or children in SC.”

“In fact, it is actively harmful,” she wrote on social platform X . “I will always support trans youth.”

Trump personally lobbied Graham to run for her late brother’s seat. Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) was a major Trump ally in Congress before his surprising death over the summer.

An average of polls on Real Clear Polling shows the race as a toss-up, with Darline Graham holding a slight lead.

Trump also hit Andrews on gun control, calling her a “vicious anti-gun radical who endorsed a ban on the most popular firearms in America.”

Andrews formerly volunteered with the South Carolina chapter of Moms Demand Action, the grassroots arm of Everytown for Gun Safety, but said at a town hall last week that she doesn’t “want to take anyone’s guns.”

“My platform to address the public health crisis of gun violence does not infringe on the Second Amendment,” Andrews said, according to the South Carolina Daily Gazette. “I support the Second Amendment, law-abiding citizens’ rights to own firearms, but I know we need to do something about this public health crisis.”

Trump pointed to her “F” rating from the National Rifle Association, in contrast to his “A” rating. The NRA has endorsed Graham in the race.

The president said Andrews is also a proponent of defunding the police. There’s no record of Andrews explicitly backing policies to defund law enforcement. She has hit Graham for not funding certain bills that would support officers.

“Our police officers put their lives on the line every day and deserve more than hollow words — they deserve a senator who will sign on to legislation that protects them and supports their families,” Andrews said in a statement earlier this month, according to reports.

Trump’s focus on culture-war issues comes as the president and his party face economic headwinds largely brought about by the war in Iran. Trump’s approval rating has hit record lows in the weeks before the midterms.

A Reuters/Ipsos survey released earlier this week found that 32 percent of U.S. adults support Trump’s job performance, while 66 percent disagreed.

The poll also showed that 37 percent of voters said Democrats have a better approach to the economy, while 33 percent said the same about Republicans. That figure is a stark change from polls taken before the start of the Iran war, which gave Republicans an edge on the economy.

articles.title: Trump’s final sprint: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Monica Alba and Garrett Haake dig into a last-minute shift in President Donald Trump’s packed campaign schedule. Plus, Megan Brand has the latest on the Alaska Senate saga. — Adam Wollner Trump shifts rally strategy in the campaign’s final days By Monica Alba and Garrett Haake President Donald Trump’s rally in Salina, Kansas, on Saturday has been canceled, according to two White House officials and a GOP source. He had been scheduled to hold a midday event at the regional airport but that is no longer happening. Instead, the president is aiming to hold “more than 20” tele-rallies between now and Tuesday, the White House officials said. This is a notable shift in strategy. Up until now, Trump has argued his in-person visits have been boosting turnout for Republican candidates and has repeatedly boasted about his heavy travel this month. As Peter Nicholas noted, Trump, 80, had been campaigning at a frenzied pace in the final stretch before Election Day. As of Wednesday, Trump had traveled on 22 of 28 days in October, appearing in a total of 19 states. He returned after midnight seven different times and, after a Western swing, got back to the White House after 4 a.m. And his rally remarks over the period averaged 1 ½ hours. No decision has been made yet on whether Trump will keep his Dubuque, Iowa, rally on Sunday, according to one of the officials. They described this change in schedule as a “shotgun approach” to hitting as many competitive races as possible in the home stretch. “President Trump will continue connecting directly with Americans nationwide through more than 20 tele-rallies before Election Day. These events give him the opportunity to highlight his accomplishments and expand his reach across the country,” one of the White House officials said. The demand for Trump’s presence has been “insane,” according to the GOP source, and his phone has been “ringing off the hook” with requests for tele-rallies. So Republicans are adjusting their approach to the president’s most precious resource — his time — in the final sprint to “maximize his reach in battleground states as races continue to tighten,” the source added. Trump is also scheduled to go to Daytona Beach, Florida, tomorrow. Today, Trump rallied in South Carolina for Republican Sen. Darline Graham, who is facing a tougher-than expected race against Democrat Annie Andrews. Alaska governor orders investigation into Peltola campaign By Megan Brand Alaska GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy announced that he is ordering an investigation into Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign after a report that it worked with allies to recruit a candidate with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in an effort to dilute his votes. The Department of Public Safety will seek to determine “whether this scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted,” Dunleavy said on X. “The evidence will determine what happens next.” Dunleavy referred to Wednesday’s revelations from a bombshell New York Times report as “disturbing new evidence” and said that “anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable.” President Donald Trump also cast doubt today on whether Republicans would seat Peltola if she wins her race. Asked by a reporter whether he thought Republicans should refuse to seat Peltola if she wins, Trump said, “You’re going to have to see what happens.” He added it was “hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.” NBC News previously reported that the second Dan Sullivan’s candidacy was under investigation by state and federal prosecutors in Alaska, and a grand jury issued subpoenas for information from witnesses linked to his campaign in August. The Justice Department also filed a lawsuit last week seeking to block the certification of the election if the incumbent Sullivan loses. Nicholas Stephanopoulos, a Harvard Law School professor specializing in election law, told NBC News that “these kinds of ‘dummy candidate’ tactics have occurred historically and generally haven’t given rise to liability.” “The tactics are certainly unsavory, but note that they’re less likely to be impactful in Alaska, because of its instant-runoff voting, than just about anywhere else. In Alaska, a confused voter just has to rank both Dan Sullivans 1-2, and then there’s no possibility of wasting her vote,” he said in an email, referring to Alaska’s ranked-choice voting. Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.
