articles.title: Republicans have knives out for Peltola as Democrats largely silent
articles.summary: Republicans are out for blood following a report that former Rep. Mary Peltola’s (D-Alaska) campaign recruited “spoiler” candidates to run on the ballot and siphon votes away from incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska). Democratic lawmakers, so far, have not come rushing to Peltola’s defense. Many in the GOP have called for legal consequences since…
articles.body:
Republicans are out for blood following a report that former Rep. Mary Peltola’s (D-Alaska) campaign recruited “spoiler” candidates to run on the ballot and siphon votes away from incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska).

Democratic lawmakers, so far, have not come rushing to Peltola’s defense.

Many in the GOP have called for legal consequences since the story broke Wednesday, and the probes are mounting.

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Peltola’s campaign and national Democrats had been involved in “ballot stacking” — recruiting extra candidates for the ballot including Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher who has garnered attention for having the same name as the incumbent senator.

The allegations come less than a week before Election Day, as Peltola appears poised to be one of Democrats’ best hopes to flip a Senate seat and, hopefully, the majority.

Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have continued to deny any involvement in the alleged scheme.

Peltola criticized the media for focusing on the story rather than on the incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan’s record.

“This is just another distraction. It’s another diversion. Everyday it’s some new, you know, ‘Look over here’ moment,” Peltola said at a campaign event Wednesday. “Anyone who’s working in your best interest isn’t going to talk about the nonsense. This is all stuff to sell newspapers. This is all stuff to get subscriptions. Nobody at The New York Times cares about affordability in Alaska.”

Democrats in general are largely staying out of the fray.

A spokesperson for Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) denied involvement in any candidate recruitment scheme but did not otherwise mention the allegations or release any statements of support.

In a CNN interview Wednesday, Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) blamed the allegations on a “disgruntled fired former campaign staffer,” noting the ballot was clear enough for voters and claims of election interference were unwarranted.

“I trust what she’s saying, she didn’t have anything to do with it,” Murphy said of Peltola. “So I’m not gonna engage in these hypotheticals. All I will say is that [President] Donald Trump is looking for a pretext to try to steal this election.”

Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) posted in support of Peltola on Wednesday but did not mention the controversy.

“I served with Mary Peltola in the House, and I know how much she cares about fighting for Alaskan families,” Kim wrote on social media Wednesday. “She’s all about fish, family, and freedom and will work to restore Alaska’s fisheries, lower the cost of gas, groceries, housing, and childcare, and fix a rigged system in Washington. She got more votes than her opponent in the non-partisan primary, and she can win this in November.”

But otherwise, there has been little noise from Democrats defending Peltola, who could face a potentially bruising floor fight with Republicans in the upper chamber if she is certified as the winner next week.

In contrast, Democrats were more vocal about backing Peltola in September when another New York Times story alleged she had mistreated and verbally berated staffers.

Republicans are hoping the new scrutiny on Peltola dents her polling advantage in time to save the incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan. But they are not waiting around, and the probes are mounting.

Republicans have been claiming for months that Democrats were involved in recruiting the other Sullivan and the new allegations have given them fresh ammo.

Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, has already launched an investigation.

“Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support,” the governor wrote on social media Wednesday. “Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections. Anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable.”

Republicans on the House Oversight Committee are also looking to probe further.

Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.), who chairs the committee, said in a press release Thursday that he has summoned two Democratic operatives named in the Times report to testify.

“Democrats are the party of fraud,” Comer said. “Knowing they can’t win on the issues, Democrats schemed to rig the U.S. Senate election in Alaska by deliberately confusing voters. This is part of a broader pattern of misconduct by today’s Democrat Party.”

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, responded to Comer in a CNN interview Thursday, saying there “should be an investigation,” but that the state should be in charge, not Congress.

“I think the state of Alaska should do its job,” Garcia said. “They should investigate any time there is accusations of any kind of issue, those should be done at the state level.”

Garcia added he thought Peltola would win and that any investigation was not likely to impact the race.

Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), who leads the National Republican Senatorial Committee, said Thursday morning that the Department of Justice (DOJ) should investigate Peltola, calling the ballot stacking “a criminal offense.”

“There’s no doubt that Mary Peltola has been, at least her campaign and the Democrat apparatus, they are involved in collusion,” Scott told NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcast partner. “They’ve been colluding together in a coordinated effort to deceive the voters.”

“I hope that the DOJ takes all the time necessary to prosecute and investigate this situation,” Scott added.

The DOJ on Thursday issued a wave of subpoenas targeting Democratic officials believed to be involved with recruiting Daniel J. Sullivan, according to ABC News .

The latest investigations come on top of a lawsuit already filed by the DOJ, at Trump’s direction, to block the state from certifying the election if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.

Ballot stacking is not an uncommon practice, and there are examples from both parties throughout history. It is also not illegal according to state law. And many voters have already voted or made up their minds about their choice. Several surveyed by Alaska Public Media on Wednesday said the reporting did not change their views or their vote, even if the allegations struck them as “icky vibes” and “kind of messed up.”

People on both sides of the aisle criticized the administration’s lawsuit, including the Republican-led state legislature . Some Democrats were vocal in standing by Peltola in that instance, and liberal groups supported a move to intervene in that case , hoping to get it dismissed.

But some of the same moderates who pushed back on the lawsuit slammed the political maneuvering.

Fellow GOP Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski said voters “deserve the honest truth” from Peltola and the campaign.

Murkowski supported Peltola in the past — though she is backing Sen. Dan Sullivan in this race— and recently endorsed a Democrat for governor. She has also criticized the earlier DOJ lawsuit to block the results.

Murkowski on Wednesday took to her long-quiet campaign account on social media with a critical post.

“While some may try to write this off as just how politics works now, ballot-stacking should have no place in our electoral process,” Murkowski said. “Run and win on your merits: your views, your policy ideas, and your accomplishments. By contrast, recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong.

“Alaskans deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign—what has been revealed is a pattern of lies and coverups and a culture of deception that belongs nowhere in our elections or among our elected officials,” Murkowski added.

articles.title: Kansas, Maine Senate races neck and neck: CNN poll
articles.summary: Democrats have narrow leads in two key Senate contests with just a few days until the election, new polls show. New surveys conducted by CNN/SSRS released Thursday found Democrats ahead in the Kansas and Maine Senate races, though both leads are in the margin of error. Both parties are spending millions on the two contests…
articles.body:
Democrats have narrow leads in two key Senate contests with just a few days until the election, new polls show.

New surveys conducted by CNN/SSRS released Thursday found Democrats ahead in the Kansas and Maine Senate races, though both leads are in the margin of error. Both parties are spending millions on the two contests in the final days of the campaign.

In Kansas, CNN found Democrat Adam Hamilton leading incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall by 4 points, 49 percent to 45 percent , among likely voters.

Hamilton has run unusually strong in Kansas, which has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in nearly 100 years. One reason Hamilton may be running ahead of Marshall is that he is viewed much more favorably than his party or his opponent. Voters have a net positive view of Hamilton by a 3-point margin, and a net negative view of Marshall by a 17-point margin.

Cost of living remains a top issue for voters in Kansas, with 43 percent listing it as their No. 1 issue.

Despite President Trump winning Kansas by 16 points in 2024, the Senate contest became competitive late in the cycle. Trump visited the state on Oct. 19 to campaign for Marshall and was due to return this weekend before the White House confirmed Thursday the president canceled Saturday’s rally , set to take place at Kansas’s Salina Regional Airport, without providing additional details about the decision.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s polling partner, gives Marshall a 58 percent chance to win reelection, characterizing the race as a “toss-up.”

In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson also leads incumbent GOP Sen. Susan Collins by a narrow 4 points , 49 percent to 45 percent, a slightly wider lead than CNN’s August poll of the race, which found Jackson ahead by 3 points.

Collins is performing unusually strong for a Republican in Maine, which former Vice President Kamala Harris took in 2024 by 7 points. Collins has a record of overperforming in the Pine Tree State, winning reelection in 2020 by 9 points even as former President Biden also won by 9 points.

The CNN poll shows that 74 percent of Collins voters are casting their ballot to support the incumbent senator. Enthusiasm for Jackson as a candidate may be lower, even among his own backers: Just 26 percent of Jackson supporters are voting to support him, while 73 percent say their vote is to oppose Collins.

DDHQ gives Jackson a 57 percent chance to beat Collins, also characterizing the race as a “toss-up.”

At the beginning of the cycle, Democrats had a slim path to a Senate majority, and it appeared nearly impossible for the party to reach 51 seats without defeating Collins in Maine.

But other paths have since opened up for the Democrats as the political environment worsens for the GOP, with polls showing them competitive in red states like Ohio, Texas, Kansas, Alaska and even South Carolina , where a poll released Wednesday showed the race tied.

DDHQ gives Democrats a 60 percent chance to flip the Senate.

The CNN/SSRS polls were conducted from Oct. 20-27 among 783 likely voters in Maine and 838 likely voters in Kansas. The polls have a margin of error of 4.5 points.

articles.title: Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad using Amy Acton’s estranged mother has ended its TV run
articles.summary: Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent for Ohio governor, is leaving the state’s airwaves, the Ramaswamy campaign confirmed Thursday.
articles.body: Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent for Ohio governor, is leaving the state’s airwaves, the Ramaswamy campaign confirmed Thursday. The ad, which debuted last week to wide bipartisan condemnation, is rotating out after completing its intended run, according to the campaign. The campaign has other ads running in the final days of the race. In the now-completed ad campaign, Donna Arthur — the mother whom Acton says she has not seen since her then-stepfather was charged with raping her as a young child nearly 50 years ago — calls her daughter a liar and urges Ohioans not to vote for her. The ad does not address details of the rape case. But critics panned the Ramaswamy campaign’s decision to use Arthur as a character witness and dredge up painful family history. “I’m learning things even about my childhood right now that I did not know,” Acton told reporters Tuesday during a campaign stop in Youngstown. “I think it is despicable. … I’m sure someday I’ll unpack everything that I’m learning here. But I’m just grateful to Ohioans and everyone, really so much support and love that we’ve received.” The Ramaswamy campaign said last week that the ad would be backed by $4 million in airtime. It began as a minutelong spot but was eventually shortened to a 30-second version. Many, including term-limited Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican who has endorsed Ramaswamy, had called on him to take down the ad. “Vivek Ramaswamy should never have run his despicable ad in the first place, and it’s totally unsurprising that he took it off the air in the most cowardly way possible, without even the hint of an apology to Dr. Acton, her family, or to the people of Ohio,” Acton campaign spokesperson Addie Bullock said in a statement Thursday. The Columbus Dispatch first reported that the ad was ending its run. “It ran to completion, and we’ve put up four other ads,” Ramaswamy said at a Thursday campaign stop, according to the newspaper.

articles.body:
Starlink drama puts spotlight on Musk’s global stature

Elon Musk and his business’s role in a recent dispute over Ukraine’s access to Starlink and its military network is putting a spotlight on the tech mogul’s outsized influence on the international stage .

Following about 10 days of confusion and finger-pointing over what caused the slowdown of Starlink and its military-grade version — Starshield — in Ukraine, Musk acknowledged his company, SpaceX, was behind the restrictions on Starlink’s commercial services.

While the exact decision behind the specific Starshield slowdown is still contested, the debacle is underscoring the vast reach the world’s richest man has on global and military affairs.

“A lot of people are uncomfortable with the idea that an individual like a corporate leader, [is] essentially making foreign policy decisions about access, though it’s not clear what the alternative is in this case,” Michael Horowitz, director of the Defense and National Security program at the Council on Foreign Relations, told The Hill.

Ukraine has used Starlink’s commercial services since the beginning of its war with Russia and later added Starshield through SpaceX’s contract with the Pentagon.

SpaceX, which was incorporated in 2002, is the largest satellite and space company, dominating the field and in turn, making Musk’s leadership even more important.

“No unelected civilian titan of industry should have the ability to interfere with a war in the way that SpaceX did here,” Andrew Grotto, director of Stanford University’s program on geopolitics, technology and governance, told The Hill.

articles.title: U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s team acknowledged screwup in case against former FBI officials
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — A top aide to U.S.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — A top aide to U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said in a Monday-night phone call that prosecutors had made a “f---up” in a high-profile criminal case against two former FBI officials, an agent who’s been investigating the case testified Thursday. The former officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, were initially charged last week with making false statements to Congress about their level of knowledge about an investigation of Hunter Biden’s laptop. A sworn affidavit attached to the complaint by Special Agent Ryan Witt cited a congressional staffer who was present for both Floris’ and Benavides’ testimony — but it turns out the person was only present for Benavides’, Witt testified at a preliminary hearing on whether there’s probable cause to charge the pair. Witt told Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui that he called the congressional staffer on Monday and was later joined on the call by Pirro aide Carlton Davis and Pirro, the top federal prosecutor for Washington, D.C. Audio of that conversation was turned over to Benavides’ attorney, Ron Safer, who read parts of the exchange in court and asked Witt whether it was accurate. At one point, Davis told the staffer, House Judiciary Committee general counsel Steve Castor, “This is our f---up,” and asked for his help finding someone who had been present for the testimony, Witt confirmed. Witt added that he still has not been able to speak to anyone who was there. Later Monday night, prosecutors filed what they called a superseding criminal complaint and a new affidavit, neither of which was signed by any law enforcement officer or judge. Faruqui tossed the complaint on Tuesday. On Wednesday, one of the attorneys for the defense asked Witt if it was unusual for a case alleging defendants made false statements to use an affidavit containing false statements — a question the judge cut off. Davis, who is listed as a special counsel in Pirro’s office, was involved in the failed effort to indict six sitting members of Congress over their comments in a social media video where they urged members of the military not to follow illegal orders. Davis previously worked as a Republican staffer on several committees, including the House Select Committee on Benghazi. Witt was on the stand in the case for a third day. He testified Tuesday that he was assigned to the case in July after FBI Director Kash Patel sent a letter directing the Kansas City, Missouri, office to look into certain people, including Floris. The direction came a day after President Donald Trump delivered an Oval Office address in which he complained that “rogue bureaucrats” had suppressed information about China’s efforts to interfere in the 2020 election, which he falsely claims was “stolen.” Both Floris and Benavides were involved in FBI efforts to secure the election and have long been targets of criticism from Trump’s allies. Witt said he was unhappy with the assignment, in part because “I had concerns that this would be viewed as political.” Witt said Wednesday that top FBI brass, including Patel, had been checking on progress in the case through in-person meetings, video conferences and updates pushed through their special agent in charge. Witt said both FBI deputy directors — Chris Raia and Andrew Bailey, who recently resigned — were involved. “The evidence in this case speaks for itself [as] to the effect that kind of pressure has on sensitive investigations like this one,” Floris’ attorney Mary Dohrmann told the judge Thursday. She said there were other mistakes in the affidavit as well, and that some of the false statements her client was alleged to have made were presented stripped of necessary context. Safer, Benavides’ attorney, told Faruqui that in most instances, calling something a political prosecution is a talking point, but not in this case. “That is the price we pay to allow politics to infect the process,” he said. The judge said he plans to issue a written ruling Monday morning.

Gasoline and energy costs rise, with inflation slightly up

Overall inflation increased slightly in September, while energy prices rose dramatically.

The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the preferred inflation metric for the Federal Reserve, rose by 0.5 percent last month and was up 3.6 percent relative to September 2025.

The price of gasoline and other energy goods rose by 9.2 percent from August to September, after increasing by 4.4 percent from July to August.

Gasoline and energy costs have risen in six of nine months this year, as the Iran war sparked oil price shocks via the Islamic Republic’s restrictions on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Food and beverage prices, meanwhile, held steady for the second straight month. The cost of food and beverages has not risen by more than 0.5 percent month over month since the start of 2025.

articles.body:
HHS begins recruiting new vaccine advisors

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is looking to revive a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) vaccine advisory panel that’s been dormant since last year, after a federal judge blocked his efforts to remake it.

The Department of Health and Human Services on Thursday published a request for nominations to the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP).

“Nominees will be selected to represent a balanced range of scientific, clinical, and public health expertise relevant to the Committee’s mission, including person(s) knowledgeable about consumer perspectives and/or social and community aspects of immunization programs,” HHS said in the notice.

ACIP makes recommendations on vaccine policy to the CDC, which help determine which shots are covered through private and government health insurance programs.

Last year, Kennedy removed all the previous ACIP members and restaffed the panel with people critical of vaccines, triggering lawsuits and states splitting off their immunization schedules from that of the federal government.

A federal judge subsequently blocked all the ACIP’s recommendations and Kennedy’s appointment of new members, finding that they appeared to “lack any expertise or professional qualifications related to vaccines or immunization as required by ACIP’s Charter.”

U.S. District Court Judge Brian Murphy in March ruled Kennedy picked “distinctly unqualified” individuals instead of experts on vaccines and immunization and disregarded the scientific process that historically underpinned the committee’s work.

Kennedy was free to try to appoint new members subject to the same legal standard, but until now the agency has not tried .

Richard Hughes IV, the attorney representing the American Academy of Pediatrics in the lawsuit against HHS, wrote in an analysis Thursday that HHS’s request “reads as a sign that Kennedy intends to appoint a committee ready and willing to continue where his previous ACIP was forced, by court order, to stop in March 2026.”

Where the agency previously asked for nominees with “expertise” in the fields of immunization practices and public health, Hughes said Thursday’s notice downplays individual expertise and emphasizes non-scientific perspectives.

Chances of severe weather are looming over certain regions across the U.S. next week, with the possibility of thunderstorms on Election Day, potentially impacting voter turnout in key races.

Parts of the Northeast have seen a long stretch of dry, warm weather in the recent days, which could extend through the weekend, AccuWeather reported . But, come Tuesday’s elections, storms are predicted to roll in.

CNN reported parts of Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Texas and Ohio could see wet weather on Election Day. In the Midwest and Plains, the rain could be accompanied by gusty winds.

There is also a possibility of rain across portions of Nebraska, Iowa, Wisconsin and Minnesota, according to AccuWeather.

In Kansas , incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R) is facing a challenge from Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton in an increasingly competitive race. Two election handicappers, Sabato’s Crystal Ball and Cook Political Report , recently shifted the race to a “toss-up.”

Michigan’s tight Senate race between GOP Rep. Mike Rogers and Abdul El-Sayed (D) has consistently made headlines this election cycle, with one recent poll leaning the contest toward the Democrat.

In north Texas, the National Weather Service’s Forth Worth office forecasts a 40 percent chance of showers and thunderstorms on Nov. 3. And in Austin, the service a similar possibility, listing a 60 percent chance of precipitation as of late October.

Texas is home to the neck-to-neck Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R). The gubernatorial contest between incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott (R) and Democrat Gina Hinojosa has also garnered attention, as President Trump has made multiple stops in the Lone Star State bolstering both Abbott and Hinojosa. Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ gives the incumbent a 68 percent chance of victory.

AccuWeather said thunderstorms with “disruptive downpours” are expected to spread into the s outheast ern U.S. this weekend but will “move away from the southern Atlantic Seaboard by Tuesday.” Atlanta, Charlotte and Miami may not see any long-lasting rain, the report said.

Ohio gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy’s (R) campaign is no longer airing a controversial ad featuring his opponent’s mother after it ran its course on the air.

The campaign previously put millions behind the ad, even after backlash from members of both parties.

The ad features Ramaswamy’s Democratic opponent Amy Acton’s mother, who calls her daughter a “liar” and tells voters not to choose her for governor of Ohio.

Acton’s campaign responded to the ad, explaining that she was removed from her mother’s custody at age 12 after being sexually abused by her stepfather, who her mother remained with until his death.

Members of both parties criticized the ad and said Ramaswamy should take it down, including Ohio’s current Republican governor, Mike DeWine.

“This ad is deeply, deeply troubling,” DeWine said. “When you know the back story … it makes it just more wrong.”

President Trump and Vice President Vance both vehemently defended Ramaswamy.

Ramaswamy said at a rally Thursday that the ad ran to completion, and that the campaign had “put up four other ads,” the Columbus Dispatch reported .

In a statement on Thursday, an Acton campaign spokesperson said Ramaswamy never should have run the ad.

“It’s totally unsurprising that he took it off the air in the most cowardly way possible, without even the hint of an apology to Dr. Acton, her family, or to the people of Ohio,” spokesperson Addie Bullock said.

The controversy over the ad drew national attention to an already expensive and highly contested race.

Ramaswamy was already behind in polling before the ad’s release, and nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives Acton a 61 percent chance to win.

articles.body:
Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif) called on Alaskan officials to investigate recent reports alleging Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign recruited her midterm opponent, Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr., to counter incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan’s (R-Alaska) reelection bid.

“Republicans and Donald Trump should certainly not be lecturing anybody on a fair election process. I think the state of Alaska should do its job,” Garcia, ranking member of the House Oversight committee, said during a Thursday CNN appearance.

“They should investigate any time there is accusations of any kind of issue. Those should be done at the state level. There’s no question.”

Garcia’s remarks come after The New York Times reported Wednesday Peltola aides and outside Democrats recruited another Dan Sullivan for Alaska’s Senate race in an effort to dilute the GOP’s vote. Peltola, a former House lawmaker, denied the allegations.

“I think there should be an investigation,” the lawmaker continued.

The California Democrat went on to note that term-limited Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.), the committee’s chair, still has “a couple more months” in office and “can certainly bring up any hearing he wants.”

Comer launched a probe Thursday into the matter, planning hearings for Nov. 5 and 6. He has called both Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager, and Jerid Kurtz, a Democratic operative the Times alleged was also involved in the operation, to appear.

“I think what’s important is it appears that whoever was involved in this was fired by the Peltola campaign over the summer. I think the state of Alaska should take any lead in investigations,” Garcia said.

The lawmaker added he believed “that this isn’t going to be a big issue on election day.”

“People understand who Dan Sullivan is. They understand who Mary Peltola is. I think we’ll see that on Tuesday,” he concluded.

The “ballot stacking” of which Peltola is accused is not illegal, GOP strategists previously told The Hill. It is a common practice for Democratic and Republican campaigns, especially in Alaska’s unusual nonpartisan, top four voting system.

Despite this, President Trump has insisted on social media Peltola should not be allowed to run for Senate due to the allegations and called for prosecution against those involved.

“The Democrats cheated! They found a man named Dan Sullivan, put him on the Ballot, then lied to the Court, and said they didn’t know anything about it. That’s perjury. She shouldn’t be allowed to run, and neither should the FAKE Dan Sullivan!” he wrote on Truth Social .
